Binary Relations
• 𝐴and 𝐵are two sets. 
• A relationship between elements of 𝐴and 𝐵can be 
represented by a collection of ordered pairs –
defined as the Cartesian product of 𝐴and 𝐵
• Since this is a relation between two sets, it is called 
a binary relation
• For a binary relation 𝑅we have 𝑅⊆𝐴× 𝐵

Cartesian Product
𝑨× 𝑩= {(𝒙, 𝒚): 𝒙∈𝑨, 𝒚∈𝑩}
• The Cartesian Product of two sets 𝐴and 𝐵is the 
set of all Ordered Pairs (𝑥, 𝑦)
• where the first element of ordered pairs “𝑥” belongs to 
first set “𝐴”
• and second element of ordered pairs “𝑦” belongs or

Properties of Relations: Reflexive
●A relation 𝑅on a set 𝐴is reflexive if (𝑎, 𝑎) ∈𝑅
for every element 
●
○For every element of a that belongs to set 𝐴, each 
element is related to itself by some relation 𝑅
●Example:
This relation is reflexive because ordered pairs 
(1,1), (2,2) and (3,3) are in the relation

Properties of Relations: Symmetric
●A relation 𝑅on a set 𝐴is symmetric if
∀𝑎, 𝑏∈𝐴[ (𝑎, 𝑏) ∈𝑅→(𝑏, 𝑎) ∈𝑅]
For every 𝑎and 𝑏in 𝐴, if (𝑎, 𝑏) is in 𝑅, then (𝑏, 𝑎) is in 𝑅
• Example:
𝐴=
1, 2, 3, 4
𝑅= {(1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,1), (2,3), (2,4), (3,1),
(3,2), (3,4), (4,1), (4,2), (4,3)}
This relation is symmetric because (𝑎, 𝑏) ∈𝑅and (𝑏, 𝑎) ∈𝑅

Properties of Relations: Transitive
●A relation 𝑅on a set 𝐴is transitive if
∀𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐∈𝐴[ (𝑎, 𝑏) ∈𝑅∧(𝑏, 𝑐) ∈𝑅→(𝑎, 𝑐) ∈𝑅]
i.e., if 𝑎𝑅𝑏, 𝑏𝑅𝑐⇒𝑎𝑅𝑐
• Example:

transitive
Because:

Equivalence Relation
• A relation on a set 𝐴is an equivalence relation if it 
is reflexive, symmetric and transitive

Closure of a Relation
• Consider constructing a new relation r+ from an 
existing relation r where r+ contains r and satisfies 
some relation property 𝑃
• The closure of a relation 𝑅with respect to property 
𝑃is the relation obtained by adding the minimum 
number of ordered pairs to 𝑅to obtain property 𝑃
• Essentially, adding the missing ordered pairs to 
make the relation meet the given property

Reflexive Closure
• The reflexive closure of a binary relation 𝑅on 
a set 𝑋is the smallest reflexive relation on 𝑋that 
contains 𝑅
• The reflexive closure S of a relation R on a set A is 
given by 
𝑆= 𝑅∪{(𝑥, 𝑥} | 𝑥∈𝐴} : the reflexive closure 
of 𝑅is the union of 𝑅with the identity 
relation on 𝐴
• The reflexive closure of a relation 𝑅on A is 
obtained by adding (𝑎, 𝑎) to 𝑅for each 𝑎∈𝐴

Symmetric Closure
• The symmetric closure of a binary relation 𝑅on 
a set 𝑋is the smallest symmetric relation on 𝑋that 
contains 𝑅
• The symmetric closure 𝑆of a relation 𝑅on a 
set 𝐴is given by
𝑆= 𝑅∪{(𝑎, 𝑏) | (𝑏, 𝑎) ∈𝑅} : the symmetric 
closure of 𝑅is the union of 𝑅with its converse 
relation
• The symmetric closure of 𝑅is obtained by adding 
(𝑏, 𝑎) to 𝑅for each (𝑎, 𝑏) ∈𝑅

Transitive Closure
• The transitive closure of a binary relation 𝑅on 
a set 𝑋is the smallest relation on 𝑋that contains 𝑅and 
is transitive
• The transitive closure 𝑆of a relation 𝑅on a set 𝐴is 
given by
𝑆= 𝑅∪{(𝑎, 𝑐) | (𝑎, 𝑏) ∈𝑅∧(𝑏, 𝑐) ∈𝑅}
• The transitive closure of 𝑅is obtained by repeatedly 
adding (𝑎, 𝑐) to 𝑅for each (𝑎, 𝑏) ∈𝑅and (𝑏, 𝑐) ∈𝑅

Transitive Closure
• Example:
Let 𝐴= {1, 2, 3} and the relation 𝑅on 𝐴
𝑅= {(1, 2), (2, 3)}
Then by the definition of a transitive closure:
𝑆= 𝑅∪{(𝑎, 𝑐) | (𝑎, 𝑏) ∈𝑅∧(𝑏, 𝑐) ∈
𝑅} = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 3)}

Types of Functions
• Functions can be classified by how they map points 
from the domain to the codomain:
• Injection (one-to-one)
• Surjections (onto)
• Bijections (one-to-one and onto)
• These properties relate to important concepts such 
as the inverse of a function

Injective Functions (one-to-one)
• Definition: A function f is one-to-one or injective
(or an injection) if each image has at most one pre-image
• It preserves distinctness: it never maps distinct elements of 
its domain to the same element of its co-domain

Surjective Function (onto)
• Definition: A function is onto or surjective if every 
element in the co-domain is mapped
• Covers the entire domain (range == co-domain)

Bijective Function (one-to-one 
and onto)
• A function is bijective (is a bijection) if it is both an 
injection and surjection
• One-to-one and onto correspondence and onto

Inverse Function
• An inverse function reverses another 
function
• The inverse function of f is the 
function that assigns an element b 
(image) belonging to B (co-domain) to 
a unique element a (pre-image) in A 
(domain)
• If the function f applied to an 
input x gives a result of y, then 
applying its inverse 
function g to y gives the result x,
• The inverse function is denoted by f-1

Inverse Function
• For a function f: X →Y to have an inverse, it must 
have the property that for every y in Y there must 
be one, and only one x in X so that f(x) = y
• This property ensures that a function g: Y →X will 
exist having the necessary relationship with f.

Inverse Function and Bijection
Why must a function be bijective to have an inverse?
Consider the case where f is not one-to-one (not injective)
How can we define the inverse? Does f-1(b) = a1 or a2?
Therefore, there is no inverse.

Arithmetic Operations with 
Functions
• We can perform arithmetic operations on functions. The result is 
a new function
Consider two functions f and g:
The sum of f and g
(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)
The difference of f and g
(f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x)
The product f and g
(f * g)(x) = f(x) * g(x) = f(x) g(x)
The quotient of f and g
(f / g)(x) = f(x) / g(x) = f(x)/g(x)

Composite Functions
• Function composition is an operation that takes 
two functions f and g and produces a new function h such 
that h(x) = g(f(x))
• Composition of functions is essentially one function is inside of 
another function
• The composition of functions is a special case of the composition 
of relations
• In composite functions the order in which the composition of 
the functions is written is important
• (f ∘g)(x) = f(g(x)), the g function is inside of the f function
• (g ∘f )(x) = g(f(x)), the f function is inside of the g function

Composite Functions
• How to find the composition of two functions:
• Rewrite the composition in a different form
• Replace each occurrence of x found in 
the outside function with the inside function
• Simplify the answer.

Composite Functions - Example
If f(x) = –4x + 9 and g(x) = 2x – 7, find (f ∘g)(x)
(f ∘g)(x) = f(g(x)) 
Rewrite the composition in a different form
= -4(2x - 7) + 9 
Replace each occurrence of x in f(x) with g(x) = 2x – 7
= -8x + 28 +9
Simplify ...
= -8x + 37

Composite Functions - Example
If 𝑓(𝑥) = – 4𝑥+ 9 and 𝑔(𝑥) = 2𝑥– 7, find (𝑔∘𝑓)(𝑥)
(𝑔∘𝑓)(𝑥) = 𝑔(𝑓(𝑥))
Rewrite the composition in a different form
= 2(−4𝑥+ 9) −7
Replace each occurrence of x in g(x) with f(x)
= −8𝑥+ 18 −7
Simplify ...
= −8𝑥+ 11
